groups.principle: State made for one thread (a count without atomics, a link others change, a Cell, module state confined to one thread) is never reached from another thread by any route: each type's thread markers follow from everything it holds or can reach, a type-erased value by what it may hold, and every route to another thread (a channel, a spawn, a scoped task's work, a thread_shared owner, an export's calling thread) needs them.
groups.shared_cause: The specification lists the thread markers and the routes one case at a time instead of deriving them from one property. THR-8's Send list and THR-9's ThreadShared list leave out sharedref mut. THR-2's routes leave out scoped tasks. THR-11 limits a task's making of shares owners but says nothing of ending them. THR-1 checks only Send and direct changes at the thread_shared line. An erased error type (AnyError) has no stated markers. FFI-33/33c confine module statics differently under `main` and `creator` with no reason given. So each new holder, route or confinement falls between the lists.

groups.principle: Everything that points into or is served by a memory manager's memory (a value made in it, anything holding one, a view, a weakref link, a count in one of its blocks) ends before the manager gives that memory back, and nothing else is ended; `using` follows every type whose value owns heap memory of its own, a program's own types included, wherever the manager can serve that memory for the value's whole life, on the thread where the value may end.
groups.shared_cause: ALC-1, TYP-46 and LT-4 tie to a manager's life only 'a value made in an instance, and every value that holds one', and give a closed list of the types `using` may follow. They do not state the property that whatever lives in or points into the manager's memory is bounded by it and given back on its thread. So a weakref link (which holds no value), a scope's views (only part of the memory is released), a thread_shared value (released on another thread, with no runtime chunk header) and String, Deque and the rest (left off the list) each fall outside, and the list contradicts its own property sentence.

groups.principle: A value is made, once, in storage that fits everything the program later does with it (a counted block if any line shares it, the thread_shared header if any line shares it between threads, writable memory if links count it), so no later line moves it or changes its header while a view, a link or a C pointer points at it, and every sharing word may follow a local of the function alike.
groups.shared_cause: HEAP-3 puts a value in its counted block at the line that shares it, and CT-5 puts a static in read-only memory. groups.principle: Safe code relies only on what the compiler checks or on a fact someone vouched for in unsafe code: every fact the compiler cannot check (what C does with a pointer, what C passes in, where a C++ reference points, whether a foreign global changes, what a header runs before main, what an unsafe body does when safe code reaches it, whether a wrapped C object is thread-safe) is refused in safe code until vouched, and one vouching spelling reaches every kind of item and every type.
groups.shared_cause: The rules that let safe code act on an unchecked fact are written per construct. FNI-10's safe-fn list checks parameters but not pointers inside a @layout(c) struct. FFI-31b types an export's C arguments as if checked. FFI-40 derives a C++ reference result's lifetime from a body that does not exist. FFI-41 exempts C++ const globals, ignores mutable members, and leaves C no way to assert. FFI-51 asks for unsafe on C imports only. UNS-1 does not reach drop or a safe virtual call landing in an unsafe override. TYP-43 vouches Send only, for structs and enums only. @ffi(handle) has no meaning. So an unchecked fact reaches safe code by an unlisted route, or a fact that could be vouched has no spelling.

groups.principle: Every end the program does not write as a call (above all a thread_shared value's drop queued back to its making thread, and any drop the compiler places) counts as a call at each point where it may run, so the lock, walk and view rules see it, and it runs within a stated bound: before the thread waits idle, leaves Ember for C, or ends.
groups.shared_cause: RC-4 point 3, a lead choice and not verdict 101, puts the check points that run queued drops at loop back edges and blocking calls. No rule counts those drops as calls there: EFF-24 counts only what code calls, and THR-20 counts the drop only on the other thread. Nothing bounds when they run on a thread that is idle in the runtime or back in C. So the same hidden end can clash with a held lock or a walk (J7-01) or never run (J7-02).

groups.principle: Ownership that crosses between Ember and C is written in Ember's own words and has one owner at every moment: what C keeps (a callback, an object's address, a raw owner) is tracked on Ember's side by an owner or token whose end releases C's hold exactly once, and what Ember takes from C (adopt) is ended by the type's own end (its drop, its C++ destructor, or the destroys(f) its declaration names).
groups.shared_cause: Part XVI defines these crossings piecemeal. FFI-21/23 give a token and an unregister requirement only to retained callbacks. FFI-52's own declaration of a kept callback breaks FFI-10. FFI-11 gives a retained non-callback pointer no safe type. into_raw has no inverse. adopt reads its end only from destroys(f), which an Ember class or a plain C++ class lacks. So several crossings have no Ember owner, no spelling, or no stated end.

groups.principle: A promise that a value does not change (a read-only name's, a let field's, a @cached result's inputs) holds against every route that can change it (another name, a weakref or sharedref mut link opened from anywhere, a call), and binds exactly while some holder could see the change, so not inside drop once the object has ended.

CLS-9a forbids every change after init, drop included, against CLS-7a. So a weakref link escapes the first three, while drop, where nobody can see, is caught by the last.

groups.principle: Every effect a written contract or layer forbids (Alloc, Panic(Explicit), RuntimeCheck(Aliasing), Nondet, heap memory in the core layer) is carried by exactly the operations that do it, decided by what the operation does and fixed by the language, never by a closed list of names or an implementation's choice, so a contract means all of, and only, what it says.
groups.shared_cause: The effect rules list their operations by name. EFF-9 says assert_disjoint is 'the one run-time alias check there is', and the Panic(Explicit) row is a list. DET-2 names 'thread completion order' and 'transcendental' functions. CLO-10 says a closure's one-word state 'may' stay inline. The core layer lists AnyError although its error lives in a heap block. Operations added since (runtime) or never named (a contested lock, cbrt, SIMD estimates, a closure's state, AnyError's block) fall between, so whether a contract accepts a program depends on a list or on the compiler.

92/105: reductions of scoped tasks are not Nondet

Panic and RuntimeCheck kinds of cast, unwrap, index, stale and count roll-over checks. Nondet of channels, atomics, try_lock, clocks, hash iteration order and float reductions. Effects through dyn calls and stored functions, and C calls.
groups.notes: J1-02, J5-10 and J6-01 are one question found three times: use J1-02's three options. Lead fix J6-03 is an instance the owner should hear: @noalloc and @nopanic(explicit) refuse a hand-over of a weakref-targeted object.

groups.principle: Every way a value is built (a constructor call, super.init, reading it back from saved data, a migration) goes through the type's one init (the one written, or the one made from its fields, visible exactly as widely as every field it sets) and gives each field exactly one value: the one the builder sets, else the field's default, else its type's.
groups.shared_cause: The memberwise constructor and field defaults are stated case by case. CLS-3 gives a memberwise constructor only to a class with no init and no base. STR-6 copies only CLS-2's E2100 sentence. STR-2 makes a default 'at each construction that omits the field'. STR-1 knows only pub and not pub. The @ser rules cover default and since=N only. So super.init over a memberwise base, a struct init that sets a defaulted field, a pub(package) field's constructor, and a @ser(skip) field each have no rule.
verdicts_involved: 74/85/97: owns on the making line for an owns field
159: a constructor's argument works as =
groups.other_places: C++ bases (super.init picks by arity and types, FFI-39b), @derive(Default), clone and copy of, enum variant construction, MOD-7's pub(read), defaults with side effects (id: int = next_id()), @noalloc inits, migrate_from (P09), and adopted objects (P08).
groups.notes: J1-07 (P06) decides the call words at a written init. Under every J1-07 option, `super.init(id=id)` over a memberwise base takes no words, so the dependency is wording only. J3-06 B changes CLS-2 for classes too: a default with a side effect no longer runs when init sets the field (C++'s member-initialiser behaviour), and whether it runs depends on init's body; say so (checklist 1, 15; MOD-9). J6-15 A reuses @derive(Default)'s rule.

groups.principle: Parallel code (scoped tasks and @parallel loops alike) has the result the same code has run one by one: every write is either to an element only one iteration or task touches (an element of any indexable container) or a reduction recognised from its ordinary spelling (+=, -=, *=, max(), min()), whose private copy starts at the operator's identity and combines in a fixed order; anything else needs a lock or an Atomic.
groups.shared_cause: PAR-2/PAR-3 for loops and THR-21 for tasks state the disjoint-write and reduction rules separately and by listed forms. Only MutSpan and SoA columns count as disjoint. Loops need reduce= declarations and tasks do not. The private accumulator is 'of the place's type' with no start value or combine for -=. max and min are listed with no spelling that compiles. So the same body gets two answers depending on loop or task, and listed reductions cannot be written.
verdicts_involved: 77: a field added to from several tasks is a reduction
92: decimal reductions allowed
93: copy of t or ref t in tasks
104: after join
105: a split sum stops where a task's own total overflows
groups.other_places: SIMD-vectorised reductions (SIMD-5's reduce= permission), jobs, |=, &= and ^=, unsigned and narrow places, mixed operators on one place, Map values, nested containers, Atomics written in a body (E7010's own help), `?` in a body (lead fix J7-20), and repeated types in view_mut (lead fix J7-12).
groups.notes: J7-10 A withdraws @parallel(reduce=...), which SIMD-5 names as the permission for a float reduction in a vectorised loop: say what then permits it. J7-09 A's `best = max(best, e)` becomes the one max spelling for tasks and loops only under J7-10 A. J7-08 keeps verdict 105's promise; A also refuses mixed operators on one place (E7007).

groups.principle: Code run while compiling is ordinary Ember under a checker that sees every access: a function means the same at compile time and at run time, unsafe code included (each access checked as it runs, never barred wholesale), and an operation that exists only while compiling (reading a source file) gives constant data and is done while compiling wherever it is written, or refused where it would run at run time.
groups.shared_cause: Part XIV states compile-time evaluation as restrictions on constructs, not as the property that compile-time code is checked ordinary code. One rule bars any function that contains unsafe code, far down its calls included. Another refuses only unsafe pointer access outside the compiler's memory. comptime.read_file is named with no result type, failure or run-time behaviour.
verdicts_involved: 60: unsafe only in unsafe blocks
118/119: unsafe code is unsafe as a whole
groups.other_places: comptime(e), static initialisers (CT-5), const evaluation, allocation and C calls at compile time, other comptime builtins (environment, file lists), a library's private unsafe code reached by a caller's comptime, and the read-only results of comptime.
groups.notes: J6-04 is a contradiction between two rules; J6-05 is an undefined builtin. Both are settled by stating what compile-time evaluation is.

groups.principle: A word that states something about a value goes on every kind of declaration where such a value can sit (runtime on a field and a lambda parameter as on a parameter and a variable, and before every held form), with one meaning.
groups.shared_cause: LT-48 and the grammar give runtime to `param` and `var_decl` only, and E3021's help names only those two. A method whose unsafe line comes from a dyn field cannot have the check on the field, and the lambda-parameter and shares forms were written in without a verdict.
verdicts_involved: 152: runtime on a parameter
157: the runtime messages
162: before a class type
163: on a variable, 'no function is needed only to carry the word'
groups.other_places: Lambda parameters and `runtime shares mut A` (J1-17's held-back parts), statics, captures, Option[dyn I] fields, array elements of dyn type, and runtime before every held form of a class or dyn type.
groups.notes: Add J1-17's held-back parts (a lambda's typed parameter, runtime before shares and shares mut forms) as further lines of this question (phase 3 reroute). The effect runtime carries is P14's.

groups.principle: An interface is usable as dyn exactly when every one of its methods can be called on any implementer with any argument its signature admits; a method that needs two values of one kind (a Self parameter, an Ord requirement) makes it unusable as dyn, and says why.
groups.shared_cause: TYP-22 makes an interface unusable as dyn only for a static method, a Self result or a generic method. A Self parameter passes, with no rule for a call on two different kinds. TYP-36 answers this for Eq only ('never equal') and says nothing of Ord.
groups.other_places: Binary operator interfaces (Add[Self]), Ord and sorting an Array[owns dyn Shape], Hash, Clone through dyn (TYP-22), `where Self: needs Sized`, and Eq's existing answer.
groups.notes: Option A keeps Eq's stated answer and refuses an interface requiring Ord.

groups.principle: Implicit conversions compose: whatever a plain T place accepts, an Option[T] place accepts as Some of it (one level only).
groups.shared_cause: TYP-5 composes conversions 'only where stated' (rule 11 after rules 1 to 4), so a value accepted by `owns dyn I`, by a function type, or by widening is refused once the place is an Option of the same type.
verdicts_involved: 85/97: owns on the making line inside an Option
groups.other_places: Option fields, arguments, returns, and values read through a view or an owns, every conversion of TYP-5 into an Option, and Result's Ok side if it ever wraps the same way.

groups.principle: A pack of types fills every type form it is written in (a tuple, a function type, once per type) to give exactly the type the form gives written out by hand, for every number of types, one and none included.
groups.shared_cause: TYP-47 defines packs only on functions, and TYP-27 says a tuple has two or more elements, so a tuple of a one-type or empty pack has no type. Verdict 115 started from the complaint that one type became `(A,)`.
verdicts_involved: 115: typed variadic generics
116: C++'s dots
117: print and friends take a pack
groups.other_places: fn(Ts...) with no types, View[Cs...] with one component, zip of one iterator, Event[] handlers, a tuple's interfaces written once for every size, and structs, classes and enums taking packs.
groups.notes: Rare in programs, but the library's own View[Cs...] and zip depend on it.

groups.principle: Lexical and line-start rules never take away a form the language offers: a token or line is read as what the grammar allows at its position (a match arm's list pattern, a tuple index after a dot), and a raw identifier reaches every word the lexer reserves, so every name a C header uses can be written.
groups.shared_cause: Text-level rules override the grammar. Verdict 155's 'every line that starts with [' refuses list-pattern arms the pattern grammar offers. Maximal munch reads t.0.1's `0.1` as a float. LEX-15 makes 'any use' of owned and self E1010 although LEX-14's r# lifts keywords.
verdicts_involved: 154: a [T] line sits right above its declaration
155: every other line starting with [ is E0100
156: a keyword used as a name is E0005, help r#
groups.other_places: Ranges `..` against `..rest`, f-strings, `#!` lines, comment lines between a [T] line and its declaration, C/C++ names that are Ember keywords (type, async, await, macro), and number literals after a dot.
groups.notes: J1-05 A narrows verdict 155: quote it. A also needs list patterns' meaning (the names are views, ..rest a Span) and a grammar that can produce [..rest]. (t.0).1 works today, so J1-15 is a corner.

groups.principle: A value that holds a resource is ended by its own drop on every path out of its scope, an early exit through `?` or return included, and that drop leaves the resource in a stated state.
groups.shared_cause: GPU-2 settles a frame that never began and a frame ended twice. Frame is not @must_drop and has no drop, so ending one without end_frame (an early `?`) leaves the acquired image and open recording undecided.
verdicts_involved: 56: an object is ended before its drop runs
57: destroying counts as calling its drop
groups.other_places: Command buffers, GPU buffers and mappings, File, Socket, lock guards, Scope and JobScope (@must_drop, THR-6), transactions, arena scopes, and callback tokens (P08).
groups.notes: Renderers meet it on every texture-load error inside a frame.

groups.principle: One idea has one spelling wherever it is written: a list of interfaces is written the same way after needs, dyn and some, and a function has the same name in std.math and in its deterministic twin.
groups.shared_cause: Two spellings of one idea, with no reason given. Verdicts 109 to 112 moved bound lists to `needs (A, B)`, but the dyn/some grammar keeps `+` because it was never asked. std.math.det calls the natural logarithm `log` where std.math calls it `ln`.
verdicts_involved: 109/110/111/112: needs everywhere a list of needs is written
133: a verdict replacing a spelling reaches every place
groups.other_places: `where` clauses, interface parents, extend lines, other det names against std.math (log2, log10, exp, pow), any other twin module, and P07's J2-11 (ref_to_ptr beside the cast).
groups.notes: For J1-13 do not widen verdicts 109-112 without the owner; show `[T: needs (Add, Copy)]` beside `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)` and say plainly that after dyn the brackets come without needs.

groups.principle: `as` converts between every pair of scalar types whose meaning is defined (a bool and a char to every integer type), and the conversion list says that it is complete.
groups.shared_cause: TYP-6 gives only char to u32 and u8 to char, nothing for bool, and unlike TYP-5 is not marked complete, so `visible as u8` and `c as int` are undecided.
groups.other_places: Floats to and from char and bool, unit-only enums (ENM-3), narrowing char casts that keep low bits as integer casts do, and conversions into bool or char (x != 0, char.from_u32).

groups.principle: A layout attribute changes only where data lives, never what an expression means: a field split into columns still reads and writes as the field.
groups.shared_cause: SOA-2 and SOA-6 define ps.f and ps[i].f by the column of f, but @soa(flatten) gives the field no column of its own, so ps.pos and ps[0].pos = v have no meaning.
groups.other_places: Nested flatten, @soa without flatten, @layout(c), packing and alignment attributes, SIMD lanes, views of columns, iteration over SoA, and hot reload of SoA layouts.

groups.principle: Every fixed capacity the language imposes fails the same way when it runs out: a stop at the line naming the capacity, and a try_ form returning an error where the program may handle it.
groups.shared_cause: FFI-53 sizes the callback table and retires worn-out slots as HND-3 retires Pool slots, but says nothing of a full table, and a registering safe fn has no error result.
verdicts_involved: 59: a count is checked before it rolls over, stopping in every profile
96: a real 8-bit counter for the limit tests
groups.other_places: Pool insert/try_insert (HND-3), owner and weak counts (RC-1, RC-4), handle generations, bounded channels, SmallArray's inline capacity, thread-local queues.
groups.notes: The example uses J8-01's spelling (P08). A 32-bit target reaches 65,536 live callbacks.

groups.principle: Each fact a declaration rests on is written in one place: the header an overlay describes is named once, and a second naming that could disagree is removed or checked.
groups.shared_cause: GRM-35 still names a header in every overlay line, the import names one, and verdict 121 records one in ember.overlays (FFI-30c applies an overlay 'only to the header it was written for'), so three places name it and nothing says which counts.
verdicts_involved: 121: the header is recorded by Ember in a package file of its own
127: every project has an ember.toml

notes:
I placed 91 items in 28 groups: 20 groups of two or more and 8 groups of one. That is the 90 confirmed owner_odr items in phase2.json other than J4-14, plus J7-05, which sits in P03 with J4-05. J4-14 is in no group. It is a lead fix carried by verdict 53, and I list it under P10's other_places because it is the same read-only promise, broken through another name of the same place.

For every item I read the title, the problem, each option's summary and the checker's reason. Where a grouping turned on details I also read the example, the outcome and the recommendation. I checked JOB.md verdicts 1 to 166 (164 to 166 are answered) and OWNER-DIRECTION.md, and checked the spec for RC-1, HEAP-3 and CT-5.

Severity is the higher of the item's phase-2 severity and its phase-3 cluster's. Ranks put memory safety first (data races, use after free, dangling views, unchecked C facts, drops that clash or never run, a lent function kept past its owner), then the weaker safety cases (reload layout, read-only promises), then what ordinary programs meet often.

The dependencies follow phase 3's order:
- K05 before K34 (inside P02).
- K12 before K31 (P06 before P08).
- K51 before K52 (P07 before P08).
- K21 before K47 (inside P07).
- K17 before K43 (inside P10).
- K22 before K23 and K26 before K62 (inside P11).
- K19 before K32 (P06 before P15, wording only).

Six placements were judgment calls:
- J5-05 is in P02 rather than P01 or P03, because of its K34 dependency. P02 depends on P01, and the notes name the P03 header link.
- J7-06 and J2-12 are in P04 (vouching is the trust boundary) rather than P01. P01's notes say that after verdict 165 they are P01's only way out for C wrappers.
- J8-13 and J8-16 are in P08 (ownership crossing to C) rather than with J7-19, which stays alone as P23.
- J1-07 is in P06 (call words) rather than P15 (construction).
- J3-07 is in P11, because a header's temporaries follow the same rule as the names it opens, per phase 3's resolution of the J1-09/J3-07 conflict.
- J8-14 is in P04 because it decides what safe code may trust about a C handle. It also shares XVI.4 with J8-08.

P11 is the largest group (12 items). It is still one rule: one table of source, word and form that decides what a name gets. Its notes split it into five facets, and phase 3 already edits those rules together.

The groups of one keep their own causes. P24 (J1-13, J6-10) is the most abstract group; it could be split into two groups of one if the designer prefers.

Phase 3's draft corrections are attached to their groups:
- P06: verdict 159 for J1-07, verdict 51 for J3-02, one spelling for K18.
- P22: verdict 155 for J1-05.
- P09: verdict 159 for J7-15's code.

- P10: J5-07's observer case.

- P15: J3-06 B's side-effect note.
